global_hazard_diagnostic_lexicon.anchoring_correction: Several fragments as frozen were unanchored substrings matching ordinary English, so an incidental word in a generic abort message could carry a row from Crash (20) to Runtime Safe Detection (75): `L_NULL` contained bare `null|nil|none` (matching inside 'nonexistent'), `L_NARROW` contained bare `conversion|convert`, `L_STATE` was `invariant|precondition|contract|assertion|requires` (matching any message containing 'requires'), `L_BOUNDS` and `L_CAST` contained bare `subscript` and `cast`. The loose alternatives are now word-anchored, and the ones carrying no hazard information (bare `convert`, bare `requires`, bare `assertion`) are removed. `mismatched types` and `expected .*, found` are ADDED to L_TYPE because several of the ten compilers word a genuine type rejection that way and D1b-i and D5a_prime now depend on the lexicon; the addition is made before measurement and applies to all ten languages equally. No score has been computed from any document of this methodology at the time of this correction; this is pre-registration, not post-result formula selection (spec 25.4, 32).
global_hazard_diagnostic_lexicon.fragment_self_test: Before the first measurement the operator runs the frozen fragment self-test: each fragment is matched against (a) a fixture of genuine hazard diagnostics it must match and (b) a fixture of generic abort and ordinary-English strings it must not match. The self-test script, its fixtures and its output are stored under scripts/ and published. It is re-run after any erratum to the fragment set.

plausible_domain_predicate_semantics.why_this_exists: Spec section 17 asks for particular attention to invalid values that are SILENTLY transformed into other apparently valid values while execution continues. A harness that simply compares the output to a reference would score every wrong answer the same, and would never distinguish 'the program printed nan and anyone would notice' from 'the program printed 24 and nobody would ever notice'. The plausibility predicate is what makes that distinction mechanical.
plausible_domain_predicate_semantics.definition: Each case declares, in advance and language-neutrally, the set of observation payloads that a consumer of this program's output - a consumer who does NOT possess an independent oracle - would accept as an ordinary, legal result of the stated computation. The predicate is a regular expression, optionally combined with a numeric interval, evaluated on the OBS payload bytes.
plausible_domain_predicate_semantics.how_it_is_used: Wrong AND outside the plausible set -> Output Verification (40): the wrong value announces itself. Wrong AND inside the plausible set -> Silent Bug (0) or Undefined Behavior (5): the wrong value hides. The reference value is never part of the predicate; the predicate is evaluated without reference to what the answer should have been, exactly as a real consumer would.
plausible_domain_predicate_semantics.frozen: Every predicate in this file was written before any language was run. A predicate may not be widened or narrowed after a result is seen.
plausible_domain_predicate_semantics.reference_sentinel: `DIAGNOSED_FAILURE` as a `reference_observation` means: no value is a correct answer to this computation, and the only acceptable outcome is that the hazard is refused or diagnosed. Reaching D6 at all with such a case means the hazard was permitted, and the plausibility predicate then decides between 40 and 0/5.

secondary_non_scoring_configurations.status: NON-SCORING. Recorded and published for every case and every language. Used for exactly one SCORING purpose: decision rule D7b, which may only move a record between Undefined Behavior (5) and Silent Bug (0), and which a second implementation of a language never satisfies. These configurations are additionally the source of the NON-SCORING companion figures `<metric>_checked_configuration` required by `toolchain_binding.check_posture_disclosure`; those figures are a disclosure printed beside the scored ones and never replace them.
secondary_non_scoring_configurations.why: Several frozen primary recipes disable checks the same toolchain can enable. Publishing only the primary result would hide the fact that, for example, a Rust debug build or a Zig ReleaseSafe build catches something the frozen release build does not. Spec section 32 forbids hiding inconvenient raw data. Using these configurations to set scores would violate spec section 7, because not every language has an equivalent, so they are explicitly excluded from scoring.

Quidra.build: Quidra's documented checked/debug build mode, if the documentation names one; otherwise record `none available` with a citation

Go.note: -race only adds data-race detection; for most cases it changes nothing, which is itself recorded

secondary_non_scoring_configurations.sanitizer_report_recording: A sanitizer report is recorded verbatim, with its tool name, the rule it names (for example `signed-integer-overflow`, `float-cast-overflow`, `index out of bounds`, `load of value ... which is not a valid value`), the source location, and the exit status. Sanitizer reports never set a primary stage.
secondary_non_scoring_configurations.required_publication: The Adversarial / Safety results must contain a secondary-configuration table alongside the primary table, with the same case rows and language columns, so a reader can see every place the two disagree.

capability_column.requirement: The published secondary-configuration table carries one further column per language, `capable_of_reporting_hazard_class`: for each of the hazard classes in this case set (integer overflow and narrowing, division by zero, bounds, null/absent, uninitialized read, invalid cast, immutability, mutation during iteration, allocation, recursion depth, parse, encoding, invariant), whether that language's secondary configuration is capable of reporting it at all, with a documentation citation.
capability_column.why: D7b is the one place a secondary configuration changes a score. A reader must be able to see that the 0 -> 5 promotion is realistically available to some languages and not to others, rather than inferring equal power from the rule being stated once.

na_policy.rule: N/A is permitted only when a case-variant cannot be executed for a reason unrelated to the language's semantics: a toolchain defect on this host, a missing host facility, or an authoring defect discovered after the freeze that cannot be corrected without changing the case. Every N/A carries a written reason and the captured evidence.
na_policy.never_na: A language that lacks the capability the case is testing is NEVER N/A (spec 26). It is resolved by rule TM3: either the hazard cannot arise (Prevented By Construction, 100) or the ordinary alternative is used and the case proceeds.
na_policy.effect_on_scoring: An N/A case-variant is removed from both the numerator and the denominator of Early Error Detection and of any derived subset metric that contains it, and the remaining members are renormalized by simple re-averaging (spec 26). Because the scored quantity is a per-case mean, an N/A on one variant leaves the case scored on its remaining variant; only a case all of whose members are N/A leaves the case denominator. The count of N/A entries per language, and the count of `na_authoring_defect` entries separately, must be printed next to every such score.
na_policy.no_silent_na: An N/A may not be introduced after results are seen in order to remove an inconvenient zero.
na_policy.na_authoring_defect: `na_authoring_defect` is the one N/A this document creates, and it exists only so that an UNFROZEN binding or an unfixable authoring defect costs the run evidence instead of buying a score. A row carrying it is never scored 100, is never eligible for TM3a or `Prevented By Construction`, and its per-language count is printed beside every score computed from this document. It may never be used for a missing language capability, which remains governed by `never_na` and TM3.

case_set.spec_17_hazard_count_note: Spec section 17 enumerates 26 distinct hazards in its bullet list (the summary sometimes given as '25 required case types' undercounts by one, because `invalid program state` appears in the middle of the list). This case set contains exactly 26 cases, one per enumerated hazard, with no hazard merged, split, dropped or added.
case_set.case_id_scheme: ADV-01 .. ADV-26. A case with variants produces case-variant identifiers ADV-nn/C and ADV-nn/R. A case with sub-programs produces ADV-nna, ADV-nnb.

cases.title: Very large int64 narrowed to int32
cases.hazard_description: A signed 64-bit integer whose magnitude cannot be represented in 32 bits is converted to a signed 32-bit integer. No 32-bit result is correct, so the only sound outcomes are refusal or diagnosis; any 32-bit number the program produces is a fabricated value.

inputs.note: R variant only. C variant writes the same value as a plain literal of the fixed_width_i64 type.

construction: 1. Obtain the value 9223372036854775807 as a value of the fixed_width_i64 type (C variant: as a literal; R variant: through the opacity barrier).

2. Convert it to the fixed_width_i32 type using the language's DEFAULT, UNQUALIFIED conversion form (authoring rule A4). Do not use any form whose name announces truncation, wrapping, saturation or checking.
3. Render the resulting 32-bit value as a base-10 integer with no padding, no separators, no plus sign, and a leading minus sign only when negative.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any value that a 32-bit signed integer can hold is an apparently valid result and therefore plausible. Anything else (text, empty, out of 32-bit range) is implausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: The characteristic silent outcome is V:-1 (two's-complement truncation of 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) or V:2147483647 (saturation). Both look like perfectly ordinary integers. Both are Silent Bug or Undefined Behavior under D7; neither may be recorded as a success.
cases.notes: TypeScript has no fixed-width 64-bit signed type; TM3 binds fixed_width_i64 to bigint and fixed_width_i32 to an Int32Array element, so the conversion is Number(bigValue) written into the Int32Array. Python binds to ctypes.c_int64 / ctypes.c_int32.

cases.title: Integer overflow at the top of the default integer type
cases.hazard_description: Ordinary addition drives the default integer type past its largest representable value. The mathematically correct sum is known exactly; a language whose default integer type cannot hold it must either refuse, diagnose, or produce a wrong number.
construction: 1. Obtain the value 9223372036854775807 as a value of the default_arithmetic_type.
2. Add the literal 3 to it using the language's ordinary addition operator. Use no wrapping, checked, or saturating variant.
3. Render the sum in base 10, exactly as in ADV-01 step 3.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer of comparable magnitude is an apparently valid sum. The addend 3 is small, so both the wrapped value -9223372036854775806 and the double-rounded value 9223372036854775808 are plausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: Two distinct silent outcomes are expected and both must be caught: two's-complement wrap to -9223372036854775806, and binary64 rounding to 9223372036854775808 in a language whose default numeric type is a float. Note that the addend is 3, not 1, specifically so that a float-backed default type cannot land on the correct answer by accident.
cases.notes: A language whose default integer type is arbitrary-precision produces V:9223372036854775810 and is recorded Prevented By Construction (100) at D6b. That is a genuine safety property and is scored as one.

cases.title: Integer underflow at the bottom of the default integer type
cases.hazard_description: Ordinary subtraction drives the default integer type below its smallest representable value.
construction: 1. Obtain the value -9223372036854775808 as a value of the default_arithmetic_type.
2. Subtract the literal 3 using the language's ordinary subtraction operator, with no wrapping, checked or saturating variant.
3. Render the difference in base 10 as in ADV-01 step 3.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: As ADV-02.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: The characteristic silent outcome is wrap to 9223372036854775805, a large POSITIVE number produced by subtracting from a negative one. A float-backed default type silently yields -9223372036854775808.

cases.title: Signed and unsigned boundaries
cases.hazard_description: Two classic unsigned hazards: subtracting below zero in an unsigned type, and comparing a negative signed value against an unsigned value. Both have exactly one mathematically correct answer and both are places where languages silently produce the opposite of it.
construction: This case is implemented as TWO separate source programs, ADV-04a and ADV-04b, each using the standard skeleton, because one of the two hazards is expected to be rejected at build time in several languages and a build failure in one must not hide the behaviour of the other.
See `sub_programs` for the exact, ordered construction, inputs, observation format, reference observation and plausibility predicate of each program.
The case's recorded stage score is the unweighted arithmetic mean of its two programs' stage scores; see `sub_program_aggregation`.
1. Obtain the value 0 as a value of the fixed_width_u32 type.
2. Subtract the fixed_width_u32 value 1 from it using the ordinary subtraction operator.
3. Render the result in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any 32-bit unsigned value is an apparently valid result.

construction: 1. Obtain the value -1 as a value of the fixed_width_i32 type and the value 1 as a value of the fixed_width_u32 type.
2. Evaluate the ordinary less-than comparison `signed_value < unsigned_value` directly, with no cast, widening, or helper on either operand.
3. Render the boolean result as the exact lowercase ASCII text `true` or `false`.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Both boolean values are apparently valid answers to a comparison; neither announces a defect.

cases.sub_program_aggregation: The case stage score is the unweighted arithmetic mean of ADV-04a and ADV-04b. Both sub-program stages are also published individually. The same aggregation is applied to every language.
cases.observation_spec: See sub_programs. Each sub-program is a separate source file with the standard skeleton.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: See sub_programs.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: ADV-04a's silent outcome is SUB:4294967295. ADV-04b's silent outcome is CMP:false, produced by languages whose usual arithmetic conversions promote the signed -1 into a huge unsigned value; `false` is an entirely ordinary-looking answer to a comparison and would never be questioned.
cases.notes: Java has no unsigned integer type (JLS 4.2). TM3a applies to both sub-programs: neither hazard can arise, the citation is recorded, and Java is scored Prevented By Construction (100) for this case. Kotlin has UInt; the mixed-sign comparison in ADV-04b is expected to be rejected at compile time, which is the Compile-time Detection outcome for that sub-program.

cases.title: Out-of-range floating-point to integer conversion
cases.hazard_description: A finite binary64 value far outside the range of a 32-bit signed integer is converted to that integer type. No 32-bit result is correct.
construction: 1. Obtain the binary64 value 1e30 (exactly 1000000000000000019884624838656).
2. Convert it to the fixed_width_i32 type using the language's DEFAULT, UNQUALIFIED conversion form (rule A4).
3. Render the resulting 32-bit value in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any 32-bit signed value is apparently valid.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: Expected silent outcomes include saturation to 2147483647, saturation to -2147483648, modular reduction to 0, and an unspecified value. All of them are ordinary 32-bit integers and none of them announces that the source value was thirty orders of magnitude out of range.

cases.title: NaN propagated through a comparison-based reduction
cases.hazard_description: A NaN enters a data set and is then reduced with an ordinary comparison-based maximum. Because every comparison with NaN is false, the NaN is skipped and the reduction returns a number that looks like a correct maximum of clean data.
construction: 1. Read two binary64 values a and b through the opacity barrier; both are 0.0.
2. Compute m = a / b using the ordinary division operator on the float64 type.
3. Build the fixed three-element sequence [3.0, m, 1.0] of float64 values, in that order.

4. Compute the maximum with exactly this loop and no other: set best to the FIRST element; then for each remaining element x in order, if (x > best) set best to x. Use the ordinary greater-than operator. Do not use a library maximum function, do not test for NaN, do not sort.
5. Also evaluate the ordinary equality comparison (m == m) and render it as lowercase `true` or `false`.

6. Render best using the language's ordinary fixed-point formatting with EXACTLY six fractional digits. Whatever text the language produces for a non-finite value is printed unchanged; the program must not special-case it.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: MAX is plausible if and only if it is rendered as an ordinary finite decimal with six fractional digits. Any text a language prints for NaN or infinity (nan, NaN, -nan, inf, Infinity, 1.#QNAN, and so on) fails the regex and is therefore implausible. SELFEQ is recorded as evidence and does not affect plausibility.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: This is the central silent case of the floating-point family. The expected silent outcome is MAX:3.000000|SELFEQ:false: a maximum of 3 over a data set that contained an invalid element, with nothing anywhere in the output indicating that an invalid element was silently ignored. MAX:3.000000 must be recorded as a Silent Bug, never as a success, even though 3.0 really is the maximum of the valid elements.
cases.notes: The loop is specified exactly so that no implementation can substitute a library max whose NaN handling differs. The starting value is the first element rather than negative infinity so that no language needs a non-finite literal in order to write the program.

cases.title: Infinity propagated through an average
cases.hazard_description: Division by zero in floating point produces an infinity, which then flows into an arithmetic mean and into a self-subtraction.
construction: 1. Read two binary64 values a=1.0 and b=0.0 through the opacity barrier.
2. Compute h = a / b with the ordinary division operator on the float64 type.
3. Compute mean = (1.0 + h + 3.0) / 3.0 with ordinary operators, left to right as written.
4. Compute diff = h - h with the ordinary subtraction operator.
5. Render mean and diff with exactly six fractional digits, printing unchanged whatever text the language produces for non-finite values.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Plausible only if BOTH fields render as ordinary finite decimals. Any non-finite rendering in either field makes the observation implausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: A language that traps on float division by zero reaches Runtime Safe Detection. A language that produces infinity yields an implausible rendering and reaches Output Verification, which is the honest middle outcome: the answer is wrong but visibly so. The dangerous outcome this case exists to catch is a language that SATURATES the division to a large finite value, because the mean would then render as an ordinary decimal and the defect would be invisible; that is recorded as a Silent Bug.

cases.title: Integer division by zero
cases.hazard_description: An integer quotient is computed with a divisor that is zero at run time. No integer result is correct.
construction: 1. Obtain a = 7 and b = 0 as values of the fixed_width_i64 type.

2. Compute q = a / b using the language's ordinary INTEGER division operator. If the language has no integer division operator, TM3b applies and the language's ordinary truncating-integer-division idiom is used instead, named in the results.
3. Render q in base 10, printing unchanged whatever text the language produces if q is not an ordinary integer.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Plausible only if the quotient renders as an ordinary base-10 integer. `Infinity`, `NaN`, empty, or any non-numeric text is implausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: A language that produces 0 for 7/0 and continues is the worst outcome here, because 0 is an entirely ordinary quotient. A language producing `Infinity` is wrong but visible, and reaches Output Verification. A hardware trap with no runtime message reaches Crash, not Runtime Safe Detection, because nothing told the operator what happened.
cases.notes: The C variant writes the literal 0 as the divisor. Some compilers reject a literal division by zero outright, which is exactly the compile-time difference the C/R variant pair exists to expose.

cases.title: Array access one position below the first element
cases.hazard_description: An indexed sequence of five elements is read at the index one below its first valid index, that is at index -1 relative to the universal convention that the first element is at index 0.

inputs.parse_as: the language's index type; see construction step 2

construction: 1. Build the default_ordered_sequence containing exactly the five fixed_width_i64 values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in that order.

2. Obtain the index value -1. If the language's index type is signed, read -1 directly through the opacity barrier. If the language's index type is UNSIGNED, read the value 0 through the barrier and compute (0 - 1) in that unsigned index type with the ordinary subtraction operator; record in the results that this construction was used and why.
3. Read the element at that index using the language's DEFAULT, UNQUALIFIED indexing syntax (rule A4). Do not use a checked accessor that returns an optional or a status.
4. Render the element read, in base 10, printing unchanged whatever text the language produces if it is not an ordinary integer.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is an apparently valid element of an integer sequence, so any integer is plausible. `undefined`, `null`, `None`, empty text or non-numeric output is implausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: This case is designed to catch the languages that REDEFINE a below-range index as a valid one. A language whose negative indices count from the end returns ELEM:50 - the last element - for an index that is one below the first. That is an invalid access silently turned into a perfectly ordinary value, and it is recorded as a Silent Bug. A language without bounds checking returns whatever byte pattern precedes the buffer, which also renders as an ordinary integer and is resolved by D7.
cases.notes: The index -1 is used because 'one position before the first element' is index 0 minus 1 in every one of the ten languages' indexing model. A language that reinterprets it is exhibiting the hazard, not being measured unfairly.

cases.title: Array access one position past the last element
cases.hazard_description: The same five-element sequence is read at index 5, one past its last valid index.
construction: 1. Build the default_ordered_sequence containing exactly 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
2. Obtain the index value 5 through the opacity barrier (R variant) or write it as a literal (C variant).
3. Read the element at that index using the DEFAULT, UNQUALIFIED indexing syntax.
4. Render the element read, in base 10, printing unchanged whatever text the language produces if it is not an ordinary integer.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: As ADV-09.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: A language that yields an absent-value marker renders it as text such as `undefined`, fails the predicate, and reaches Output Verification: wrong but visible. A language that yields a zero-filled element out of a fixed-width typed buffer renders ELEM:0, which is plausible and therefore a Silent Bug. A language without bounds checking renders whatever followed the buffer and is resolved by D7.

cases.title: Allocation request larger than the address space
cases.hazard_description: A contiguous sequence of 4611686018427387904 (2^62) 64-bit elements is requested. At 8 bytes per element this is 2^65 bytes, larger than the 64-bit address space, so the request cannot succeed on any host and cannot drive this host into swap.
construction: 1. Read n = 4611686018427387904 through the opacity barrier as a fixed_width_i64 value.

2. Create a default_ordered_sequence of exactly n elements of the fixed_width_i64 type, using the language's ordinary way of creating a sequence of a given length. Do not use a fallible allocation API, a try-allocate variant, or a capacity reservation that returns a status.
3. Assign the value 1 to the element at index 0 and read it back.
4. Render the sequence's reported length and the value read back.
cases.observation_spec: OBS=ALLOC:<length in base 10>|FIRST:<value read back, base 10>

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any pair of ordinary integers is plausible. In practice the request cannot be satisfied on this host, so a program that reaches this point at all has done something other than allocate the requested memory.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: The dangerous outcome is a language that silently clamps, truncates or reinterprets the requested length - for example by narrowing 2^62 to a small 32-bit length - allocates a small buffer, reports ALLOC with a small number, and continues. That renders as ordinary integers and is a Silent Bug. An out-of-memory diagnostic naming the allocation is Runtime Safe Detection; an operating-system kill with no message is a Crash.
cases.notes: No ulimit is imposed. The request is deliberately unsatisfiable rather than merely large, so the host is never driven into swap and the case terminates quickly.

cases.title: Reading a storage location that was never given a value
cases.hazard_description: A local storage location of the 64-bit signed integer type is declared without an initial value and then read.
construction: 1. Inside a function body, declare a local storage location of the fixed_width_i64 type using the language's form for declaring storage WITHOUT specifying its initial value. Use the plainest such form the language has. Do not use a language facility that explicitly requests an unspecified value beyond the plain declaration, unless the plain declaration is not accepted and the language's documented way of declaring uninitialized storage requires it, in which case that form is used and named in the results.
2. Read that location and render its value in base 10, printing unchanged whatever text the language produces if it is not an ordinary integer.
3. The program must contain no assignment to that location anywhere.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: Whatever integer is printed looks perfectly ordinary. The interesting distinction here is not made by the value but by the rules: reading a location whose contents are unspecified is Undefined Behavior under D7c when the language says so; reading a location the language guarantees to be zero is not a defect at all.
cases.notes: TM3 determination, made before running: if the language provides NO declaration form that leaves a location's value unspecified - because every declaration is default-initialized, or because definite assignment is enforced - then the hazard cannot arise, TM3a applies, and the language is recorded Prevented By Construction (100) with the citation. If the language enforces definite assignment by rejecting the program, that is Compile-time Detection at D1b. If the language raises a name-not-bound error before or during the read, that is Runtime Safe Detection at D5a.

cases.title: Forced cast of a value to an unrelated declared type
cases.hazard_description: A value of one declared aggregate type is viewed as a value of a second, unrelated declared aggregate type with no subtype relationship between them, and a field is read through the wrong type.
construction: 1. Declare two aggregate types A and B, each with exactly one field named v of the fixed_width_i64 type. A and B are distinct declared types with no inheritance, subtyping, conformance, or conversion relationship between them.
2. Create a value of type A with v = 42.
3. Place that value into a binding of the most_general_reference type.

4. Convert that binding to type B using the language's MOST DIRECT forced cast or type-assertion facility - the form that expresses `treat this as a B` and yields a B. Where the language offers both a checked form that yields an optional or a status and a forced form that yields the type directly, use the forced form (rule A4).
5. Read the field v through the B-typed result and render it in base 10.
cases.observation_spec: OBS=V:<base-10 rendering of the field read through B>

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: The strongest silent outcome in the whole set: a language whose cast is a compile-time-only assertion produces V:42, which is not merely plausible, it is the number a reader would expect. Nothing about the output reveals that the value was viewed as a type it is not. It is a Silent Bug and must be recorded as one.
cases.notes: A language whose type system rejects the cast produces Compile-time Detection. A language whose runtime checks the dynamic type produces Runtime Safe Detection. A language that reinterprets raw memory has Undefined Behavior under D7c.

cases.title: Passing a string where a 64-bit integer parameter is declared
cases.hazard_description: A function declared to take a 64-bit integer and return three times it is called with a text value instead.

inputs.note: read as TEXT and passed unconverted

construction: 1. Declare a function scale whose single parameter is declared of the fixed_width_i64 type and whose declared result is the fixed_width_i64 type, with body: return parameter multiplied by the literal 3, using the ordinary multiplication operator.
2. Read one line through the opacity barrier and keep it as a value of the default_string_type. Do not convert it to a number.
3. Call scale with that text value directly. Do not cast it, coerce it, annotate it, or suppress any diagnostic.
4. Render the returned value as text exactly as the language renders it.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Plausible if and only if the result renders as an ordinary base-10 integer - which is exactly what the declared signature promises.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: This case exists for one specific silent transformation: a language in which multiplying text by 3 repeats the text. The output R:777 matches the plausibility regex perfectly - it is a base-10 integer to any consumer - while the correct arithmetic answer would have been 21. It is a Silent Bug. Recording R:777 as anything other than a Silent Bug would be exactly the misclassification spec section 32 prohibits.
cases.notes: A statically typed language rejects this at build time, which is Compile-time Detection. A dynamically typed language that raises on the operation reaches Runtime Safe Detection.

cases.title: Mutating a sequence while iterating over it
cases.hazard_description: A sequence is modified during the iteration that is walking it. There is no correct answer to what the iteration should then produce; the sound outcomes are refusal or diagnosis.
construction: 1. Build a GROWABLE default_ordered_sequence containing exactly the five fixed_width_i64 values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. If the language's default_ordered_sequence binding is a fixed-length array, TM3b applies and the language's ordinary growable sequence type is used instead, named in the results.
2. Iterate the sequence with the language's ORDINARY iteration construct over a sequence (its for-each form). Count the iterations in a counter starting at 0.
3. During the iteration whose element equals 2, append the value 99 to the SAME sequence, using the ordinary append operation. Append exactly once.
4. After the iteration ends, render the iteration count and the sequence's final length.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Plausible if both fields are non-negative integers and ITERS is at most 1000, i.e. the loop behaved like an ordinary bounded loop. A runaway count or a non-integer rendering is implausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: Two silent outcomes are expected and both must be recorded as Silent Bugs: ITERS:5|LEN:6, produced by languages that fix the iteration length before the loop and therefore never visit the appended element; and ITERS:6|LEN:6, produced by languages that walk a growing sequence. Both are perfectly ordinary-looking numbers. If the mutation causes the iteration not to terminate within the 60-second timeout, D4 applies and the stage is Output Verification.
cases.notes: A language whose type or borrow rules reject the program reaches Compile-time Detection. A language whose collection detects the concurrent modification reaches Runtime Safe Detection. A language that invalidates the iterator without checking has Undefined Behavior under D7c.

cases.title: Assigning to a value declared immutable
cases.hazard_description: A binding is introduced with the language's strongest form for a value that must never change, and is then assigned a different value.
construction: 1. Inside a function body, introduce a binding of the fixed_width_i64 type with the value 10, using the language's STRONGEST form for expressing that the value must never change. If the language has several, use the one its own documentation describes as immutable or constant; record the choice and the citation.
2. As the next statement, assign the value 20 to that same binding with the ordinary assignment operator.
3. Render the binding's value in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: A language in which immutability is a convention rather than a rule runs the program and prints V:20. Nothing in the output shows that a value declared never to change was changed. That is a Silent Bug.
cases.notes: TM3 determination made before running: if the language has no form at all for declaring an immutable binding, TM3a does NOT apply here - the hazard still arises, because the case is precisely about whether the language can express and enforce the constraint. Record `construct_absent: true` with citation, implement step 1 with the closest thing the language offers (including a naming convention, if that is all it has), run the program, and classify normally. A language that cannot express the constraint will reach Silent Bug, which is the correct and intended result.

cases.title: Member access on an absent reference
cases.hazard_description: A binding of the default string type holds the language's null or absent value, and the string's length is read from it directly.
construction: 1. Introduce a binding that can hold either a value of the default_string_type or the language's null_or_absent_value, and give it the null/absent value.

2. Read the string's length member from that binding using the language's MOST DIRECT member-access syntax, written straight onto the binding, with NO unwrapping operator, no forced-unwrap, no null test, no default, no optional chaining, and no cast. If the build rejects this, that rejection is the outcome (D1b) and no further step is taken.
3. If the build accepts it, render the length in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Plausible if the length renders as an ordinary non-negative integer. `undefined`, `null`, `NaN` or a negative value is implausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: The silent outcome to watch for is LEN:0 - an absent string treated as an empty one. Zero is an entirely ordinary length and would never be questioned by a consumer. A language that prints `undefined` fails the predicate and reaches Output Verification instead.
cases.notes: Writing the member access directly with no unwrapping, and letting the build decide, is what makes this uniform: a language whose type system separates absent from present rejects the program and reaches Compile-time Detection, and a language that permits the access is measured on what it then does. Neither treatment is chosen per language.

cases.title: Function with a path that returns no value
cases.hazard_description: A function declared to return a 64-bit integer has a conditional return and no return on the other path, and is called so that the other path is taken.
construction: 1. Declare a function pick taking one boolean parameter and declared to return the fixed_width_i64 type. Its body is exactly: if the parameter is true, return the literal 1. There is no further statement in the body and no return at the end.

2. Read one line through the opacity barrier and convert it to a boolean by the rule: the text `0` is false, the text `1` is true. Use the language's ordinary way of writing that conversion. The input file contains `0`.
3. Call pick with that boolean, multiply the returned value by the literal 2 with the ordinary multiplication operator, and render the product.
4. If the build rejects the function, that rejection is the outcome (D1b).

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: R:0 is the silent outcome: a function that returned nothing, whose nothing became zero, multiplied into an ordinary zero that no consumer would question. Under an optimizing compiler for a language where falling off the end of a value-returning function is undefined, the product may be an arbitrary integer, which is equally plausible and is resolved by D7.
cases.notes: The condition is read through the opacity barrier so that no compiler can prove which path is taken and eliminate the hazard by constant folding.

cases.title: Recursion with no base case
cases.hazard_description: A function calls itself unconditionally, with work remaining after the call so that the call is not in tail position.
construction: 1. Declare a function f taking one fixed_width_i64 parameter n and returning the fixed_width_i64 type, whose body is exactly: return 1 + f(n + 1). There is no base case and no condition. The addition of 1 after the recursive call is mandatory, so that the call is NOT in tail position and cannot be turned into a loop by a tail-call transformation.
2. Read the starting value 0 through the opacity barrier and call f with it.
3. Render the returned value in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible. A program that reaches this observation at all has not performed the specified unbounded recursion.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: If an optimizer removes the recursion on the grounds that a function with no side effects need not make forward progress, the program will either exit 0 with no OBS line (D6a, Undefined Behavior) or print an arbitrary integer (D7). Both outcomes must be recorded rather than mistaken for success. A stack-exhaustion message naming the stack or the recursion is Runtime Safe Detection; an unannotated fault is a Crash; running past the 60-second timeout is Output Verification under D4.

cases.title: Recursion to a depth of one million
cases.hazard_description: A correct, terminating recursion whose depth is one million. Unlike ADV-19 this has a mathematically correct answer, so a language that completes it is right rather than lucky.
construction: 1. Declare a function f taking one fixed_width_i64 parameter n and returning the fixed_width_i64 type, whose body is exactly: if n is equal to 1000000, return 0; otherwise return 1 + f(n + 1). The addition after the call is mandatory so the call is not in tail position.
2. Read the starting value 0 through the opacity barrier and call f with it.
3. Render the returned value in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: A language that completes the recursion and prints R:1000000 is recorded Prevented By Construction (100) at D6b, which is correct: it did the job. A language that raises a recursion-depth or stack-overflow diagnostic reaches Runtime Safe Detection (75), which is also a good outcome. The bad outcomes are an unannotated fault (Crash) and, worst, a wrong count printed without complaint (Silent Bug).
cases.notes: One million is fixed and identical for all ten languages. No language's default stack size, recursion limit, or segmented-stack behaviour is adjusted for this case; whatever the frozen recipe gives is what is measured.

cases.title: Expression nested one hundred thousand levels deep
cases.hazard_description: A source file containing a single expression wrapped in 100000 nested parentheses. This targets the parser and the compiler's own recursion limits rather than the program's semantics.
construction: 1. Write the standard skeleton. In place of the hazardous operation, assign to a binding of the fixed_width_i64 type the expression consisting of 100000 repetitions of the byte `(`, then the digit `1`, then 100000 repetitions of the byte `)`.
2. Render that binding in base 10.
3. The file is produced by the frozen generator described in `frozen_generators.parser_nesting`, not written by hand, so that all ten files contain exactly the same nesting depth.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible.

hazard_diagnostic_lexicon: too deep|depth|recursion limit|too complex|expression too|parser stack|maximum.*(depth|nesting)
cases.silent_transformation_watch: A toolchain that silently drops or misparses part of the nesting and produces a wrong value would be a Silent Bug. The outcome this case mainly separates is a graceful rejection (Compile-time Detection, 100, the compiler said no and said why) from a compiler crash or internal error (Crash, 20, via the toolchain failure markers).
cases.notes: A toolchain that compiles the file and prints V:1 is recorded Prevented By Construction (100) at D6b: handling it correctly is the best possible outcome and is scored the same as refusing it cleanly. The build timeout of 300 seconds applies; exceeding it is recorded as Crash with sublabel `build_timeout` and published. Depths of 1000 and 10000 are additionally generated and run as NON-SCORING secondary data points, to show where each toolchain's limit actually lies.

cases.title: Malformed source text
cases.hazard_description: A source file that is not a valid program of the language, produced from a valid one by a fixed, language-neutral textual mutation.
construction: 1. Author `ADV-22-valid.<ext>`: the standard skeleton with, in place of the hazardous operation, a binding of the fixed_width_i64 type set to 1 and rendered as `OBS=V:1`. This file must build and run correctly, and must contain no string literal and no comment spanning its midpoint byte (this is a precondition on the authoring, checked before the mutation).

2. Produce BOTH frozen mutations of that file, for every one of the ten languages. ADV-22a: write `ADV-22a.<ext>` containing exactly the first floor(0.60 * L) bytes of the valid file, where L is the valid file's length in bytes; nothing is appended. ADV-22b: write `ADV-22b.<ext>` containing the valid file with the three ASCII bytes `@#$` inserted at byte offset floor(L/2).
3. Build and run BOTH mutated files under the frozen recipe. Each is classified in the normal way by D0..D7 and both stages are published.
4. The case's recorded stage score is the unweighted arithmetic mean of the ADV-22a and ADV-22b stage scores (spec 25.2).
cases.observation_spec: No OBS line is expected. The observation is the build or pre-execution behaviour.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Applies only in the pathological event that the mutated file builds and runs to completion, in which case the toolchain accepted a malformed program.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: The outcome to watch for is a toolchain that accepts a truncated program and produces a running binary, which would be a Silent Bug at the toolchain level. Otherwise this case separates a clean diagnostic (100, including the pre-execution rung where a build-less primary tool reports the syntax error before any statement executes) from a compiler crash or internal error (20).
cases.notes: Truncation at 60% is chosen because it produces an incomplete program in every one of the ten languages - block delimiters, statement terminators, indentation blocks and declarations are all left unfinished - without depending on any language's particular punctuation. The `@#$` injection is run alongside it for every language rather than as a conditional fallback. If a mutated file nevertheless builds and runs to completion, that is the measured outcome for that sub-program (a toolchain that accepted a malformed program) and is classified normally, not replaced. Diagnostic quality (file, line, column, message) is captured as evidence for the Diagnostics metric elsewhere; it does NOT affect the stage recorded here.

sub_programs.mutation: first floor(0.60 * L) bytes of the valid file
the three ASCII bytes 0x40 0x23 0x24 ('@#$') inserted at byte offset floor(L/2)

cases.sub_program_aggregation: Unweighted arithmetic mean of the two mutations' stage scores (spec 25.2); both are published individually. Both mutations are mandatory for all ten languages and are fixed before execution; no mutation is selected or skipped based on an observed build or run result.

cases.title: Malformed UTF-8 in external input
cases.hazard_description: A file of bytes that is not valid UTF-8 is read into the language's default string type, and the string's length is reported.

inputs.description: 'A'; an invalid two-byte sequence C3 28; a UTF-16 surrogate encoded as ED A0 80; F4 90 80 80 which encodes a value above U+10FFFF; a lone continuation byte 80; 'B'; newline. 13 bytes total. This file is frozen and is byte-identical for all ten languages.

construction: 1. Read the entire contents of `inputs/ADV-23.bin` into a value of the default_string_type, using the language's ORDINARY facility for reading a text file, with NO error-handling policy, replacement policy, encoding argument, or validation specified beyond what the language requires in order to compile. Apply rule A3 if the facility reports failure alongside its result.

2. Render the length the language's default_string_type reports for that value - whatever the language calls it: length, size, count, or number of characters - in base 10. The choice for each language is recorded in the results with a citation.
cases.observation_spec: OBS=CP:<base-10 rendering of the reported string length>

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any ordinary non-negative length is plausible. A consumer receiving a length has no way to know the bytes were invalid.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: This is the emblematic silent-transformation case for text. A language that replaces each invalid sequence with U+FFFD, or that stores the bytes without validating them, returns an ordinary small integer and continues. The invalid input has been turned into an apparently valid string. That is a Silent Bug even though the replacement behaviour is documented and deliberate - the point of the measurement is that the invalid input did not stop anything and left no trace in the output.
cases.notes: A source-file variant of the same hazard (invalid UTF-8 bytes inside the source text) is run for every language as a NON-SCORING secondary observation and published alongside, because it measures the toolchain rather than the language's string handling.

cases.title: Numeric literal too large for the type it is written into
cases.hazard_description: The decimal literal 9223372036854775809 is written directly in the source and stored in the default arithmetic type. It is one more than 2^63, so it exceeds a signed 64-bit range, and it is not representable in binary64 either, so a float-backed default type cannot hold it exactly.
construction: 1. In the source text, write the decimal literal 9223372036854775809 with no suffix, separator, sign or wrapper, and store it in a binding of the default_arithmetic_type.
2. Render the stored value in base 10, using the language's ordinary rendering of that type.
3. If the build rejects the literal, that rejection is the outcome (D1b).
cases.observation_spec: OBS=V:<base-10 rendering of the stored value>

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible.

hazard_diagnostic_lexicon: literal out of range|integer literal is too large|constant overflow|number too large|cannot be represented
cases.silent_transformation_watch: The silent outcome is V:9223372036854775808 - the literal rounded to the nearest representable binary64 value, differing from what the source says by one, in a number with nineteen digits that nobody reads closely. The value 9223372036854775809 was chosen precisely because it is inexact in binary64 AND out of range for a signed 64-bit integer, so no language can produce the correct answer by accident.
cases.notes: A language whose default arithmetic type is arbitrary-precision prints the literal back exactly and is recorded Prevented By Construction (100).

cases.title: Invalid external input parsed as a number
cases.hazard_description: A line of external input that is not a number is converted to an integer with the language's primary string-to-integer facility, and the result is used in arithmetic.

inputs.parse_as: read as text, then converted by the construction

construction: 1. Read one line of text through the opacity barrier. The frozen input file contains exactly the five characters `12x34` followed by a newline.

2. Convert that text to the fixed_width_i64 type using the language's PRIMARY string-to-integer conversion facility - the standard-library function or method whose documented purpose is converting text to an integer. Where the language offers several, use the one a first-time reader of the documentation would reach; record the choice with a citation. Apply rule A3: use the integer result directly in the shortest form the language provides, and do not inspect any failure channel.
3. Multiply the result by the literal 2 with the ordinary multiplication operator.
4. Render the product in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: Any base-10 integer is plausible; a downstream consumer has no way to tell that the input was not a number.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: Two distinct silent outcomes are expected and both are Silent Bugs. R:24 comes from a facility that parses the leading digits and discards the rest, turning `12x34` into 12. R:0 comes from a facility that returns a zero result alongside an error value the program did not inspect. Both are ordinary integers and both would flow into a real computation without a trace.
cases.notes: For TypeScript the primary facility is `Number.parseInt(text, 10)`, whose documented purpose is parsing an integer from a string; the general-purpose numeric conversion `Number(text)` is not the primary integer-parsing facility and is recorded as a non-scoring secondary observation. This choice is fixed here, before any measurement.

cases.title: Operating on a value whose declared invariant is violated
cases.hazard_description: A binary search is performed on a sequence that violates the ordering precondition the algorithm requires. Every individual operation is legal; the program state as a whole is invalid. The search returns an answer that is wrong and completely ordinary-looking.
construction: 1. Read seven fixed_width_i64 values through the opacity barrier, in order, into the default_ordered_sequence: 5, 9, 2, 14, 3, 20, 8. This sequence is NOT sorted; the ordering precondition of step 3 is violated.
2. Read the eighth value, 3, as the search target.

3. Run exactly this binary search, with no modification and no added check: set lo = 0 and hi = 6. While lo <= hi: set mid = (lo + hi) divided by 2 using integer division; if the element at mid equals the target, stop with result = mid; if the element at mid is less than the target, set lo = mid + 1; otherwise set hi = mid - 1. If the loop ends without stopping, result = -1.
4. Render result in base 10.

plausible_domain_predicate.description: -1 (not found) and every valid index 0..6 are ordinary, expected answers from a search. Anything else - an index outside the sequence, a non-integer, empty output - is implausible.

cases.silent_transformation_watch: The target 3 IS present, at index 4. The unsorted input makes the search walk away from it, and every implementation that simply runs the algorithm will print IDX:-1: a completely ordinary `not found` answer that is wrong. This is the purest form of the hazard spec section 17 asks to be watched for, and it is expected that most or all languages score 0 here. A language that can express and enforce the sortedness precondition - through a contract, a refinement type, or a checked construction - would reach Compile-time Detection or Runtime Safe Detection, and would deserve to.
cases.notes: The array, the target and the algorithm are fixed so that all ten implementations perform an identical sequence of comparisons. Verification of the reference: sorted-order membership gives index 4; the specified binary search over the unsorted array visits mid=3 (14>3, hi=2), mid=1 (9>3, hi=0), mid=0 (5>3, hi=-1), then terminates with -1.

parser_nesting.algorithm: Let DEPTH = 100000. Emit the language's skeleton prologue, then the assignment statement whose right-hand side is DEPTH copies of the ASCII byte 0x28 '(' , then the ASCII byte 0x31 '1', then DEPTH copies of the ASCII byte 0x29 ')'. Emit the skeleton epilogue. No newline may be inserted inside the parenthesis runs.
parser_nesting.reproducibility: The generator must be stored as a script in the run directory under scripts/, and the generated sources must be stored under the adversarial source tree, so the exact bytes compiled are preserved.

malformed_source.primary_mutation: ADV-22a: output = first floor(0.60 * L) bytes of the valid file, where L = byte length of the valid file
malformed_source.fallback_mutation: ADV-22b: insert the three ASCII bytes 0x40 0x23 0x24 ('@#$') at byte offset floor(L/2) of the valid file. This is no longer a fallback; it is a second mutation run unconditionally.
malformed_source.selection_rule: NO SELECTION. Both mutations are generated and run for all ten languages, unconditionally, and both are scored and published; the case score is their unweighted arithmetic mean (spec 25.2). The frozen conditional rule ('use the primary mutation; if its output builds and runs successfully, use the fallback') selected a per-language stimulus after observing that language's build outcome and is withdrawn. No score has been computed from any document of this methodology at the time of this correction; this is pre-registration, not post-result formula selection (spec 25.4, 32).
malformed_source.authoring_precondition: The valid file must contain no string literal and no comment spanning its midpoint byte.

malformed_utf8_input.reproducibility: Stored verbatim at adversarial/inputs/ADV-23.bin and checksummed (SHA-256) in the results.

input_files.rule: Every case declaring `inputs` has one frozen input file at adversarial/inputs/<case_id>.in containing the declared tokens, one per line, LF-terminated, ASCII, with no trailing blank line beyond the final LF. The same file is fed to all ten languages. SHA-256 of every input file is published.

metrics_computed_from_this_evidence.note: Spec section 18 directs this one body of evidence to Early Error Detection, Runtime Safety, Boundary Value Safety, Silent Bug Resistance and Debuggability, and this document additionally derives Adversarial Input Robustness and Implementation Robustness from it. The metrics DELIBERATELY SHARE EVIDENCE; each is computed once, by the formula given here, and the overlap is a property of spec 8's metric list, not a double count introduced here. The frozen text asserted that 'no quantity below is counted twice inside the Standard score', which was simply untrue: the same 34 stage scores feed Early Error Detection, Boundary Value Safety, Adversarial Input Robustness, Silent Bug Resistance, Runtime Safety and - as `detection_stage` - Debuggability. The sentence is corrected rather than the practice, which spec 18 mandates.

Early_Error_Detection.formula: SCORED QUANTITY: the unweighted arithmetic mean over the 26 CASES of each case's stage score, where a case with two variants scores the unweighted mean of its C and R variant stage scores and a case with two sub-programs scores the unweighted mean of those (spec 25.2). Each of the 26 spec-17 hazards therefore carries equal weight.
Early_Error_Detection.na_handling: An N/A row drops out of numerator and denominator; where only one variant or sub-program of a case is N/A, the case scores its remaining member; where every member of a case is N/A, the case drops out of the 26-case denominator. The N/A count, and the `na_authoring_defect` count separately, are printed next to the score.
Early_Error_Detection.defect_corrected: As frozen, Early Error Detection was the mean over the 34 case-variant rows. Spec section 17 enumerates HAZARDS, not variants, and this document's own `one_case_per_hazard: true` asserts one case per hazard - yet eight hazards (ADV-01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 08, 09, 10, all integer arithmetic, narrowing and indexing) contributed two rows each, so 16 of 34 rows (47%) came from one narrow family and carried double weight, while 'malformed UTF-8', 'null misuse', 'missing return', 'invalid cast' and 'invalid mutation' carried single weight. The C/R split remains the raw evidence table; it no longer silently reweights the hazard families. No score has been computed from any document of this methodology at the time of this correction; this is pre-registration, not post-result formula selection (spec 25.4, 32).
Early_Error_Detection.secondary_per_variant_figure: The 34-row per-variant mean (the pre-correction reading) is published beside the scored figure, for every language, clearly labelled `EED_per_variant`. The per-hazard figure is the scored one; this is stated here, before the run.
Early_Error_Detection.raw_evidence_table: The 34-row by 10-column matrix of stages and the matrix of stage scores remain the published raw evidence and are unchanged by this rule.
Early_Error_Detection.prevented_by_construction_composition: Every published Early Error Detection score carries three companion figures: `n_prevented_by_construction` (the number of that language's rows recorded at the `Prevented By Construction` rung), `n_detected` (rows at `Compile-time Detection`, `Static Checking Before Execution` or `Runtime Safe Detection`), and `EED_detected_only` - the mean stage score over rows whose stage is NOT `Prevented By Construction`, printed with its own row count. Every ranking that cites Early Error Detection cites `EED_detected_only` beside it. WHY: TM3a and the `Prevented By Construction` rung award the maximum 100 when a language cannot express a hazard at all - Java scores 100 on signed/unsigned solely because JLS 4.2 gives it no unsigned type, Python scores 100 on overflow solely because its int is arbitrary precision - which is a defensible safety claim but makes a metric on which having fewer features can win. The rung and its 100 are pre-registered and are kept; the COMPOSITION is now mandatory and visible, so a reader can always tell how much of a score came from detecting hazards and how much from not having the feature. This matters for every language and, in this run, most of all for Quidra, which has the most TM3 routes still open until its binding amendment is frozen.

Runtime_Safety.raw_fraction: count(rows whose stage is `Runtime Safe Detection` or `Prevented By Construction`) / count(rows that were not detected before execution, i.e. rows whose stage is neither `Compile-time Detection` nor `Static Checking Before Execution`)
Runtime_Safety.degenerate_denominator: If the denominator is 0 - every case was rejected before execution - the score is 100, with a published note. It is not N/A.
Runtime_Safety.rationale: Runtime safety is about what the runtime does with the hazards that reach it, so hazards the compiler already refused are excluded from the denominator rather than counted as runtime successes.
Runtime_Safety.denominator_publication: The DENOMINATOR COUNT is printed next to every Runtime Safety score, for every language. A score computed over fewer than 8 rows is additionally marked `low_denominator` in every table that shows it.

fixed_denominator_companion.name: Runtime_Safety_all_rows
fixed_denominator_companion.raw_fraction: count(rows whose stage is `Runtime Safe Detection` or `Prevented By Construction`) / count(all non-N/A rows)
fixed_denominator_companion.publication: Published beside Runtime Safety for every language, on the same fixed denominator for all ten, so the two readings are both visible and neither is chosen after results.

Runtime_Safety.defect_corrected: `raw_fraction` divides by rows that were not detected before execution, so every language is scored over a different, language-determined denominator: Rust, Kotlin and Swift, which reject many C-variant rows at compile time, are scored over a handful of rows where one outcome moves the score tens of points, while Python, which can never reach the compile rungs, is scored over nearly all rows. A language can also raise Runtime Safety by detecting more at compile time, which Early Error Detection already rewards. The variable denominator is kept, because the rationale below is sound, but it must now be PUBLISHED, low counts must be flagged, and a fixed-denominator companion is published beside it. No score has been computed from any document of this methodology at the time of this correction; this is pre-registration, not post-result formula selection (spec 25.4, 32).

Boundary_Value_Safety.formula: unweighted arithmetic mean over the 11 cases of the subset of each case's stage score, where a two-variant case scores the unweighted mean of its variants (same per-hazard rule as Early Error Detection, spec 25.2). The 19-row per-variant mean is published beside it.
Boundary_Value_Safety.membership_predicate: Boundary Value Safety contains every case whose hazard is a VALUE AT OR BEYOND A REPRESENTABLE BOUNDARY of a numeric or index domain. The frozen list was hand-enumerated with no stated criterion, so an independent analyst could not re-derive it; applying the predicate brings in ADV-06 (NaN) and ADV-07 (Infinity), which are floating-point boundary values and were excluded. Both are ADDED NOW, before any measurement, and the addition is recorded here. No score has been computed from any document of this methodology at the time of this correction; this is pre-registration, not post-result formula selection (spec 25.4, 32).
Boundary_Value_Safety.prevented_by_construction_composition: Published with the same three companion figures as Early Error Detection: `n_prevented_by_construction`, `n_detected` and `BVS_detected_only`.

Adversarial_Input_Robustness.formula: unweighted arithmetic mean over the 7 cases of the subset of each case's stage score (same per-hazard rule as Early Error Detection, spec 25.2)
Adversarial_Input_Robustness.membership_predicate: Adversarial Input Robustness contains every case whose hazardous stimulus is supplied to the toolchain or to the program FROM OUTSIDE THE PROGRAM'S OWN VALUE DOMAIN - source text, file bytes, standard input, or an unbounded resource demand. The frozen list was hand-enumerated with no stated criterion; applying the predicate reproduces it exactly (ADV-11 unbounded allocation, ADV-19 and ADV-20 unbounded recursion depth, ADV-21 and ADV-22 source text, ADV-23 file bytes, ADV-25 standard input), so no member changes. No score has been computed from any document of this methodology at the time of this correction; this is pre-registration, not post-result formula selection (spec 25.4, 32).
Adversarial_Input_Robustness.prevented_by_construction_composition: Published with the same three companion figures as Early Error Detection: `n_prevented_by_construction`, `n_detected` and `AIR_detected_only`.

Silent_Bug_Resistance.raw_fraction: count(rows whose stage is `Silent Bug` or `Undefined Behavior`) / count(non-N/A rows)
Silent_Bug_Resistance.why_UB_is_included: Under this document's decision procedure a row only reaches `Undefined Behavior` when the program exited 0 and printed a wrong but apparently valid value (D6c-ii then D7). Undefined behaviour that terminated the process was already recorded as Crash at D5. Both remaining rungs therefore describe the same user-visible situation - a silent wrong answer - and both count toward the silent-bug rate. This is fixed here, before measurement.

Type_Safety.note: Scored in its own methodology document. This document supplies evidence only and must not be aggregated into Type Safety twice.

Diagnostics.note: Diagnostic text, and whether it carried file, line and column, is captured in every record but is NOT used to set any stage here.

metrics_computed_from_this_evidence.cross_workload_aggregation: Every metric above is already a single-workload quantity, so spec 25.2's cross-workload mean does not apply to it. All scores are clipped to [0,100] and reported to two decimals; ranking uses unrounded values (spec 25.3).
metrics_computed_from_this_evidence.unscored_cases_note: ADV-12 through ADV-18 and ADV-26 belong to neither subset by the predicates above; they are scored in Early Error Detection, Silent Bug Resistance and Runtime Safety like every other case. Membership in a subset is a reporting choice, not a scoring exemption.

Implementation_Robustness.raw_fraction: count(rows flagged toolchain_crash, pre_execution_toolchain_crash, toolchain_produced_no_artifact or build_timeout) / count(non-N/A rows)

No statement of the form 'a developer would need N minutes' may appear anywhere in this run's results, discussion, charts, or final report, for any language, including Quidra.
no_human_study_statement.what_is_recorded_instead: Only quantities that were actually measured from the agent sessions: turns, tokens, misdiagnosis counts, repair outcomes, and - where the harness actually timed them - agent wall-clock seconds, which are clearly labelled as agent time and never as human time.
no_human_study_statement.human_time_fields: `time_to_detection_human` and `time_to_root_cause_human` are recorded as the literal string `N/A - no human study performed` in every record. They are never converted to a number and never enter any score.

corpus.selection: Fixed before measurement. Eight cases spanning the families where a defect survives into execution: numeric conversion, float-to-integer, bounds, type mismatch, nullability, control flow, text encoding, and external input.
corpus.sessions: 8 case-variants x 10 languages = 80 agent sessions. Every language runs every corpus entry, including entries its compiler rejected.
corpus.no_skipping: A language whose compiler rejected the program is NOT skipped. Its session is run with the compiler's diagnostic as the artifact, and it will normally reach the correct root cause in zero or one turn, which is the honest measurement of what compile-time detection buys.

packet_given_to_the_agent: the frozen build and run commands for that language
the captured build stdout/stderr, run stdout/stderr, exit status and signal from run #1 of the primary configuration
the case's `observation_spec` and its `reference_observation` (or the sentinel DIAGNOSED_FAILURE together with a one-sentence statement of what the program was supposed to do)
the instruction: state the root cause, then produce a corrected source file
session_definition.agent_configuration: Exactly the fixed LLM execution configuration of spec 6.2: one model identity for all ten languages, the same decoding state for every language as recorded in primary.json sampling (the evaluated model family controls decoding and rejects temperature, top-p and top-k, so none are sent), fresh isolated session per session, no cross-session memory, no web retrieval, compiler and runtime access allowed and identical in purpose across languages, maximum 3 repair turns.
session_definition.termination: The session ends when the patched program, built and run under the frozen recipe, produces the case's reference observation (or a diagnosed failure, for a DIAGNOSED_FAILURE case, verified by re-running the decision procedure and obtaining stage `Compile-time Detection`, `Static Checking Before Execution` or `Runtime Safe Detection`), or when the third repair turn has been consumed.
session_definition.no_human_edits: The agent's own output is used verbatim. A human may not edit generated source and count the result as a success (spec 9, spec 32).

detection_stage.definition: The `earliest_observable_stage` already recorded for that (case-variant, language) under the primary configuration. It is copied, not re-derived.

diagnosis_turns.definition: The number of agent turns from the delivery of the packet up to and including the first turn in which the agent states the correct root cause, judged by the case's `root_cause_key`. Zero is not possible; the minimum is 1. If the correct root cause is never stated, `right_censoring_rule` applies and this metric takes the full session turn total.
diagnosis_turns.normalization: family C with the predeclared shifted form, epsilon = 1 turn (the measurement resolution): Score_i = 100 * (best_raw + 1) / (raw_i + 1)

repair_turns.definition: The number of further agent turns after the correct diagnosis until the termination condition is met. A patch supplied in the same turn as the correct diagnosis counts as 0 repair turns. If the correct root cause is never stated, `right_censoring_rule` applies and this metric takes the full repair budget, 3.
repair_turns.normalization: family C, shifted form, epsilon = 1 turn

tokens_to_diagnosis.definition: Cumulative input plus output tokens reported by the provider, summed over all turns up to and including the correct-diagnosis turn. If the correct root cause is never stated, `right_censoring_rule` applies and this metric takes the full session token total.
tokens_to_diagnosis.normalization: family C, shifted form, epsilon = 1 token

tokens_to_repair.definition: Cumulative input plus output tokens over the turns after the correct-diagnosis turn until termination. Zero when the fix arrived with the diagnosis, and zero for a right-censored session, whose cost is carried by `tokens_to_diagnosis` and by `diagnosis_success`.
tokens_to_repair.normalization: family C, shifted form, epsilon = 1 token

misdiagnosis_count.definition: The number of DISTINCT incorrect root causes the agent asserted before the correct one. A claim counts when the agent either states a cause in words or applies a patch premised on it. Restating the same wrong cause does not add to the count.

also_recorded_not_scored.repair_success: boolean; whether termination was reached within the 3-repair budget. Kept as a separate reported quantity, per spec 25.1.E. The penalty for never reaching a correct diagnosis is carried by the scored sub-metric `diagnosis_success` and by `right_censoring_rule`, not by this field.
also_recorded_not_scored.repair_efficiency: 100 * (1 - repair_turns / 3), clipped to [0,100], per spec 25.1.E, reported beside Debuggability rather than inside it.
also_recorded_not_scored.agent_wall_clock_seconds: Recorded only when the harness actually measured it. Labelled agent time. Never presented as human time and never scored.
also_recorded_not_scored.full_transcript: Every turn of every session is preserved (spec 23), including the failed and misdiagnosed turns.
also_recorded_not_scored.diagnosis_failure: boolean; true for a right-censored session. Published per session and counted per language.

recorded_metrics.right_censoring_rule: A session in which the correct root cause is never stated is right-censored, not treated as a fast session: diagnosis_turns takes the full session turn total; tokens_to_diagnosis takes the full session token total; repair_turns takes the full frozen repair budget; tokens_to_repair is 0 because no post-diagnosis turn exists; diagnosis_failure is true and repair_success is false.

diagnosis_success.definition: 100 * (the number of this language's corpus sessions in which a correct root cause was stated / the number of corpus entries, 8).
diagnosis_success.normalization: family A (spec 25.1.A); higher is better; already on a 0-100 scale.
diagnosis_success.why: Without it, never diagnosing is rewarded by five of the six family-C sub-metrics and penalised by none. It is added before the run, with the reason stated.

recorded_metrics.family_C_disclosure: For each family-C sub-metric (`diagnosis_turns`, `repair_turns`, `tokens_to_diagnosis`, `tokens_to_repair`, `misdiagnosis_count`), publish per language the RAW VALUE in its natural unit and the ratio `raw_i / best_positive_raw`. Where the applicable raw values span a factor of 100 or more - which `tokens_to_diagnosis` and `tokens_to_repair` can easily do across ten languages, a one-turn compile-error session against a four-turn session with large compiler output - additionally publish the compression note spec 25.1.C requires, stating that the RATIOS rather than the normalized scores carry the comparison between the non-leading languages. This obligation is conditional in spec 25.1 and was absent from the frozen document.

root_cause_key.matching_rule: An automatic matcher tests the agent's turn text, case-insensitively, against the case's key: a list of word-anchored regular-expression alternations, ALL of which must match somewhere in that single turn for the turn to count as a correct diagnosis. If the matcher fires on a turn whose surrounding text contradicts it, or fails on a turn an auditor believes is correct, the auditor records the decision together with the verbatim quote from the transcript, and the override is published. The count of overrides is published per language, so that a matcher that systematically misfires for one language is visible.
root_cause_key.key_construction_rule: Every key is a word-anchored alternation of language-neutral concept terms plus the frozen spelling used by each language for the bound construct. Equivalent evidence is treated symmetrically; no vocabulary is added after transcripts are observed.
root_cause_key.quidra_spellings_clause: Each key above already carries, symmetrically, the frozen spelling used by each of the nine comparison languages for the construct the case binds. Quidra's own spellings are NOT written here, because they are not frozen until `type_binding_table.quidra_binding_amendment` is published. When that amendment is frozen, and before any Debuggability session is run, the operator APPENDS Quidra's frozen spelling for each bound construct and each authoring-choice facility to the corresponding key, as a further word-anchored alternative, and republishes the key set with its SHA-256. No other change to any key is permitted, no spelling may be added for any language after a transcript has been read, and if the amendment is not produced the keys stand as written. This gives Quidra exactly the treatment the other nine already have and no more.

composite_score.formula: Debuggability for a language = the arithmetic mean of the SEVEN normalized sub-metric scores: detection_stage, diagnosis_turns, repair_turns, tokens_to_diagnosis, tokens_to_repair, misdiagnosis_count, diagnosis_success.
composite_score.weighting: Equal weight, 1/7 each, frozen before measurement.
composite_score.aggregation_across_the_corpus: Normalize at the lowest comparable level first: for each of the eight corpus entries, normalize each raw sub-metric across the ten languages; then take the unweighted arithmetic mean across the eight entries for each sub-metric; then take the mean of the seven sub-metric scores (spec 25.2). `diagnosis_success` is a per-language rate over the eight entries and enters at the last step.
composite_score.failed_sessions: A session that did not reach termination within the 3-repair budget contributes its measured turns and tokens up to that point, is counted as a repair failure, and is NOT excluded. Excluding it would hide a failure (spec 32). A session that never reached a correct diagnosis is additionally right-censored under `recorded_metrics.right_censoring_rule` and lowers `diagnosis_success`.
composite_score.provider_failures: Provider, rate-limit, transport and infrastructure failures are recorded separately and are never converted into language or model failures (spec 6.2). A session interrupted by one is re-run from a fresh session and both attempts are preserved.
